title: The Bear Just Served Its Final Course — and the Critics Are Calling It a Masterpiece
excerpt: Jeremy Allen White's last shift in the kitchen earned a 98% Rotten Tomatoes score, and the entire final season is streaming now on JioHotstar and Hulu
body:
There is a moment in the fifth and final season of **The Bear** where everything that has been simmering for four years — the grief, the ambition, the dysfunction, the desperate, furious love that binds the Berzatto family — comes roaring to a boil. It happens in Episode 7, and according to *Radio Times*, it is "the most tearful, joyful, human hour of television you'll see anywhere this year."

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=ojjCvICC86c</youtube>

That is not a small claim. But then, nothing about **The Bear** has ever been small.

The final season dropped in its entirety on **June 26** — eight episodes, no weekly drip, the whole gorgeous, agonising feast laid out at once on **JioHotstar** in India and **Hulu** in the US. And the verdict is in: a **98% Certified Fresh** score on Rotten Tomatoes from 41 reviews, making it the third-highest-rated season in the show's history, behind only the perfect 100% of Season 1 and the near-mythical 99% of Season 2.

> "In his final act of legerdemain, Storer and his team have created a fitting sendoff to one of the most intimate series in modern television." — AV Club

**Christopher Storer**, the show's creator and spiritual heartbeat, has stripped Season 5 down to its bones. The entire season — save the finale — takes place over the course of a single day. No celebrity cameos shoehorned in for Instagram buzz. No experimental detours into unrelated timelines. Just **Carmen "Carmy" Berzatto** (**Jeremy Allen White**), **Sydney Adamu** (**Ayo Edebiri**), and **Richie Jerimovich** (**Ebon Moss-Bachrach**) trying to survive one last, impossible service with no money, no food, and a ticking clock.

The setup, as *Collider* puts it, is essentially ***The Pitt*** meets ***24*** in a Chicago kitchen. After Season 4's emotionally devastating finale — where Carmy told his team he planned to walk away from everything they had built — the restaurant is bleeding out. Uncle Jimmy's countdown has expired. The finances are gone. The pantry is nearly empty. What follows is eight episodes of controlled chaos, the kind only Storer can orchestrate: a high-wire act where plumbing disasters become punchlines, and a gruelling dinner service becomes a meditation on what it means to show up for the people who need you.

The performances are staggering. **Jeremy Allen White** has never been more quietly devastating — a man who has spent his entire adult life running from his family's dysfunction only to discover that family, in all its messy glory, is the only thing worth fighting for. **Ayo Edebiri** radiates a new authority as Syd steps into the role Carmy has vacated, carrying the weight of the restaurant on shoulders that refuse to buckle. And **Ebon Moss-Bachrach** — God, Richie — finds depths of tenderness and ferocity that should guarantee him another Emmy conversation.

**Abby Elliott**, who plays Natalie "Sugar" Berzatto, told *Decider* that the show's ending left her "at peace." "These character stories feel very honest," she said. "It doesn't feel like TV. It feels like people you know and love."


The critical consensus is nearly unanimous. *Digital Spy* called it "a wonderful epilogue," while *JoBlo* declared, "There are few runs of episodes I can think of that deliver as well as this last season." The audience score, while still early, sits at 84% — and the superfans are already calling it a return to the show's Season 1 heights.

## Where to Watch

For Indian viewers, all five seasons are streaming on **JioHotstar**. In the US, it's on **Hulu** and available through **Disney+**. In the UK, the show streams on **Disney+**. All eight episodes of Season 5 are available now — no waiting, no weekly releases, just pure uninterrupted excellence.

If you haven't started **The Bear** yet, you have one of television's greatest achievements waiting for you. If you have, you already know: this kitchen was always about more than food. It was about whether broken people can build something beautiful together.

The answer, it turns out, is yes. And it is breathtaking.
